standard.title: Australia's Changing Identity and International Relationships
standard.description: the effects of global influences on Australia's changing identity as a nation and its international relationships
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have studied Australia's international relationships and identity to Year 9 level, including the development of national identity through WWI and the interwar years.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students investigate the effects of global influences on Australia's changing identity as a nation and its international relationships from the 1970s to the present.

nodes.label: Foreign policy and national identity — Whitlam to Hawke
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can investigate how the foreign policies of Whitlam, Fraser and Hawke shaped Australia's national identity through cultural exchange, migration, trade and defence.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe the foreign policy orientation of at least two of Whitlam, Fraser and Hawke and explain how each shaped Australia's national identity.
nodes.typical_width: Investigate the broad foreign policy and international relations policies of Whitlam (1972–1975), Fraser (1975–1983), and Hawke (1983–1991) in relation to cultural exchange, migration, trade and defence; explain how each government's approach shaped how Australians understood their nation's place in the world; trace the gradual shift from a primarily British-oriented identity to a more Asia-Pacific and multicultural identity.
wider: Compare the foreign policy visions of these three prime ministers, evaluating the extent to which shifts in Australia's international orientation reflected genuine value change vs responses to changing global circumstances
Investigate Whitlam's recognition of the People's Republic of China (1972) as a pivotal moment in Australia's Asia-Pacific engagement, examining its domestic reception and long-term consequences

response_modes.reason: Foreign policy analysis requires students to distinguish between stated values (what governments said they stood for) and policy outcomes (what they actually did). Structure the analysis around this distinction to build genuine evaluative skill.

success_criteria: Describe the foreign policy approach of at least two of Whitlam, Fraser and Hawke
Explain how each approach shaped Australia's national identity in relation to at least one of: cultural exchange, migration, trade, or defence
Trace the broad shift in Australia's international orientation from the 1970s to the early 1990s

nodes.label: Cultural globalisation and Australian identity
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can discuss the changing nature of Australian cultural industries and investigate Australia's contribution to international popular culture.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe how at least two overseas cultural influences shaped Australian cultural industries, and describe Australia's contribution to international popular culture in at least one domain.
nodes.typical_width: Discuss the changing nature of Australian music, film and television under overseas influences — rock 'n' roll, disco, punk, grunge, indie and other music genres; Hollywood, Bollywood, animation film industries in China and Japan; satellite broadcast; investigate Australia's contribution to international popular culture in music, film, television and sport, and the recognition of Australian creative and performing arts internationally; discuss the recognition of Australian creative and performing arts internationally.
wider: Investigate the international recognition of First Nations Australians' arts — Aboriginal visual art, Bangarra Dance Theatre, First Nations music and film — examining how First Nations cultural expression has contributed to Australia's international cultural identity and how this recognition has intersected with rights and sovereignty claims

Examine the role of social media and digital platforms in both importing overseas cultural influences and enabling Australian artists to reach global audiences without traditional intermediaries, analysing how this changes the relationship between national identity and cultural globalisation

response_modes.reason: Australian cultural industries are most productively taught as a two-way exchange — overseas influences shaping Australian culture, and Australian cultural output contributing internationally. The First Nations dimension of Australian cultural export is a significant and underexplored aspect of this bidirectional exchange.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The international recognition of First Nations arts and the digital transformation of cultural globalisation both offer rich analytical opportunities that connect cultural history to contemporary questions about national identity, sovereignty, and the changing nature of the culture industries.
success_criteria: Describe how at least two overseas cultural influences shaped Australian cultural industries
Describe Australia's contribution to international popular culture in at least one domain
Explain how cultural globalisation has both shaped and been shaped by Australian national identity

nodes.label: Rising Asia and digital connectivity
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can discuss the rising economic and political influence of China and India and examine the role of digital media in shaping Australian society and global relationships.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe the rising influence of China and India since the end of the Cold War and explain how digital media has changed Australia's global relationships.
nodes.typical_width: Discuss the rising economic and political influence of China and India since the end of the Cold War and the implications for Australia's trade, foreign policy, and identity; examine the role of digital media, including social media, in shaping Australian society — how it has changed how Australians consume news, engage in political debate, and connect to global events and communities.
wider: Examine Australia's relationship with China since the late Cold War period in depth — tracing how economic interdependence, cultural exchange and strategic tension have together created a complex relationship with major implications for Australian identity and foreign policy

Investigate a specific case of social media's role in shaping Australian engagement with a global event (e.g. climate activism, Black Lives Matter), evaluating how digital connectivity changes the relationship between national identity and global movements

response_modes.reason: This node integrates the foreign policy themes of Node 1 and the cultural globalisation themes of Node 2 with contemporary digital connectivity, completing the picture of how global influences have shaped and continue to shape Australian identity — and bringing the course's narrative up to the present.

success_criteria: Describe the rising economic and political influence of China and India since the end of the Cold War
Explain at least two implications of China's and India's rising influence for Australia
Explain how digital media and social media have changed how Australians engage with global events and relationships
